sections.title: The Prohibition of Mentioning the Name of Idolatry Respectfully
sections.html:
There is a mitzva to destroy idolatry and uproot it from the land, and this includes a mitzva to treat it with contempt and to express this by calling it by a derogatory name, as it is stated (Devarim 12:3): "And you shall tear down their altars, and break their pillars, and burn their asherim with fire, and cut down the carved images of their gods, and you shall destroy their name out of that place." Destroying the name is done by changing their name to a derogatory one, as it is stated (ibid. 7:26): "You shall utterly detest it and utterly abhor it, for it is a banned thing." Thus, if they used to call it 'Beit Galya', an expression of loftiness, one changes it to 'Beit Karya', an expression of lowliness; and if they called it 'Ein Kol', one changes it to 'Ein Kotz' (Avoda Zara 45b; 46a; SA [YD] 146:15). Likewise we have learned in the Torah and the Prophets that the idols are called 'gilulim' and 'shikutzim', expressions of contempt.

In addition, the Torah forbade vowing or swearing in the name of idolatry, as it is stated (Shemot 23:13): "And the name of other gods you shall not mention; it shall not be heard from your mouth." One who vows is one who says: "By the name of such-and-such an idol, these fruits shall be forbidden to me by a vow." One who swears is one who says: "By the name of such-and-such an idol, I swear that I will not eat these fruits," or "that I have repaid my debt" (Sanhedrin 60b; 63b). One who vows or swears in the name of idolatry is liable to lashes. And although in general one is not liable to lashes for a sin committed through speech, because of the severity of the prohibition of idolatry and the severity of vows and oaths, one is liable to lashes for this speech (Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 5:11; Kesef Mishneh there; SA YD 147:1).

Included in the prohibition is not to mention the idols in a respectful manner, for anyone who mentions them respectfully strengthens their status and transgresses a Torah prohibition. Likewise, it is forbidden to cause a gentile to swear in the name of his idols (see above 11:3-4).

Even in a neutral manner the Sages forbade mentioning them, for the very mention of them involves a kind of recognition of their existence, whereas in truth one must nullify them. Even when there is a benefit in doing so, it is forbidden to mention them. Therefore, one who wishes to set a meeting place with his friend, even when it would be convenient for him to explain that it is beside a certain idol, should not mention its name, but should find another way to explain where they will meet (Sanhedrin 63b; Rosh; SA 147:1).1

sections.title: Derogatory Names and the Ways of Peace
sections.html: The instruction to call idolatry by a derogatory name was said with regard to internal Jewish discourse; but when the derogatory words will be heard by a gentile and will offend him, one must take care not to hurt him, because of the ways of peace (darkhei shalom). This is an a fortiori inference: if they instructed to greet an idolater on his festival day in a subdued manner because of the ways of peace (Gittin 62a; below, halakha 6), all the more so one should not disparage him. All the more so when he is a decent gentile who worships idolatry involving shituf, whose faith one must not offend in word or deed. Therefore, today, when anything written or recorded can reach all the nations, the mitzva to destroy the name of the idols is fulfilled through a polite and precise explanation of their shortcomings.2

sections.title: Further Laws Regarding Mentioning the Name of Idolatry
sections.html:
It is permitted to mention an idolatry that is written in the Tanakh without calling it by a derogatory name, for since it is permitted to say the names of the idols in the Torah reading and in the study of Tanakh, it is permitted to say them always (Sanhedrin 63b; SA 147:4). In addition, it is permitted to mention the names of idols whose worship has ceased from the world.3

It is permitted for Jews living outside the Land to say the addresses of towns and streets named after idols or after 'that man', since in this context it is the name of a town or street and not of idols or houses of worship. The meticulous made an effort to change the name slightly, but when they needed to write the address of the place precisely, they wrote it as it is.

Many customarily avoid mentioning the name of Jesus (Yeshu), since the Christians made him into an object of idolatry, and when necessary they call him 'that man', thereby emphasizing that he was a man and not God. However, by the letter of the law it is permitted to say 'Yeshu', since it is a name that was given in the past to many people in Israel, and not the name of an idol.4

sections.title: The Foreign Date by the Christian Count
sections.html:
The custom of Israel is to use the Hebrew date, which expresses faith in God, Creator of the world, and whose months are the months according to which the festivals are set. In the modern era, when commercial and scientific ties between cities and countries became numerous and ramified, a growing need arose to use an agreed date in letters, in documents and in the press. And since the Christian countries were the leading ones, the date accepted among them became the date used throughout the world. Following this, Jews who came into contact with gentiles began to use it as their main date. Several of the great sages of Israel protested sharply against them, claiming that they were being drawn after the culture of the gentiles and using an idolatrous date, since this date marks the time of the birth of 'that man', whom the Christians made into an object of idolatry (Derashot Ḥatam Sofer vol. 2, 315a; Maharam Schick YD 171).

However, already then, the view of the vast majority of poskim was that although ideally it is preferable to use a Hebrew date and not a foreign one, when there is a need it is permitted to use the foreign date, since it is used in a secular context and without mentioning that it is counted from the birth of 'that man' (Tzitz Eliezer 8:8). Some added that according to the historians it is not counted from the birth of 'that man', for in truth he was born some four to seven years before the beginning of their count (Aseh Lekha Rav 6:55; Yabi'a Omer vol. 3, YD 9).

Today, following the development of means of transportation and communication, all countries have become connected to one another by countless ties, and the need to use an agreed international date for commerce, contracts, e-mail, interpersonal communication, news and history has increased. As a result, the use of the foreign date has become a constant need, and its religious context has faded away. Therefore, halakhically it is permitted to use it without restriction, while taking care to mention the Hebrew date as well. And so we find in recent generations that rabbis who were connected to the general public regularly mentioned in their letters, in addition to the Hebrew date, the foreign date as well. So did Rav Goren and Rav Shalom Messas, and so did many rabbis in the United States. The meticulous refrain from mentioning the foreign date without need, or else note 'according to their count'.5

sections.title: Lo Teḥonem – Gifts and Praise
sections.html:
The Torah commanded Israel to keep away from idolaters, so that they not learn from their ways, as it is stated (Devarim 7:1-4): "When the Lord your God brings you into the land which you are entering to possess it, and casts out many nations before you… seven nations greater and mightier than you; and the Lord your God delivers them before you and you smite them, you shall utterly destroy them; you shall make no covenant with them, nor show them favour. Nor shall you intermarry with them… for he will turn away your son from following Me, and they will serve other gods; and the anger of the Lord will be kindled against you, and He will destroy you quickly." The essence of the mitzva of 'Lo teḥonem' ("nor show them favour") is not to be gracious to the seven nations of Canaan or to have mercy on them, but rather to destroy them utterly so that they not cause Israel to sin; however, included in the mitzva is a general warning to keep away from idolaters, so that we not learn from their ways. Three Torah prohibitions are included in the mitzva of 'Lo teḥonem': 1) not to give them a place of encampment (ḥanaya) in the Land of Israel; 2) not to give them grace (ḥen), that is, not to praise them; 3) not to give them a free gift (matnat ḥinam) (Avoda Zara 20a). In this halakha we will deal with the prohibition of giving grace and a free gift.

Some say that these prohibitions apply only to idolaters, but according to most of the later poskim these prohibitions apply to any gentile who does not observe the seven Noahide commandments.

The prohibition against giving a gift or praise to a gentile applies when there is no benefit in it for the Jew, so that it expresses excessive closeness to a gentile who does not observe the seven Noahide commandments, which are his basic moral obligations. But when the gift or the praise brings benefit to the Jew, there is no prohibition (SA 151:11). Therefore, it is permitted to give a gift to a neighbour, to an employee or to someone with whom one does business, because through the gift the neighbour will maintain good neighbourly relations, the employee will want to work diligently, and the one who comes to buy from him or sell to him will want to continue doing business with him. Likewise, it is permitted to give a tip to a taxi driver or a waiter. In frameworks such as these it is also permitted to give a generous gift, as is customary among generous people, but not beyond that.

The same law applies to words of praise: it is permitted for an employer to praise his workers in order to encourage and guide them. Likewise, for the sake of a moral benefit it is permitted to relate a good deed done by a gentile, as the Sages praised the Persians for their customs of modesty and courtesy, and Dama ben Netina for his honouring of his father (Rabbi Ḥayim Palagi in Nishmat Kol Ḥai YD 55).6

As for a resident alien (ger toshav), since he observes the seven Noahide commandments, it is a mitzva to give him a gift and to praise him. We also learned that it is permitted to give him a gift from what is stated (Devarim 14:21): "You shall not eat anything that dies of itself (nevela, an animal that was not slaughtered according to halakha); you may give it to the stranger who is within your gates, that he may eat it."7

sections.title: Gifts and Greetings on Their Festival Day
sections.html:
Although we learned that it is permitted to give a gift, as is customary, to an acquaintance who is an idolater, the Sages forbade sending him a gift on his festival day, for out of his sense of satisfaction at having received a gift on his festival day, he is likely to give thanks to his idol; it would then turn out that the Jew caused this and transgressed what is stated (Shemot 23:13): "And the name of other gods you shall not mention; it shall not be heard from your mouth." But if he knows that the idolater will not give thanks to his idol for it, it is permitted to send him a gift on his festival day, as Rava sent a gift to Bar Sheshakh on his festival day (Avoda Zara 65b; Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 9:2; SA 148:5; Beit Hillel 1).

Likewise, the Sages forbade entering the home of an idolater on his festival day and greeting him with 'shalom', for one thereby causes him to give thanks to his idol (Gittin 62a, and Rashi), and perhaps one may even be drawn after him (Meiri). And if one met him on the way on his festival day, so that they not come to enmity, he should say 'shalom' to him "in a subdued voice and with a solemn manner." But on an ordinary day he should greet him with a pleasant countenance. "They said of Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai that no one ever greeted him first, not even a gentile in the marketplace" (Berakhot 17a), and an ordinary gentile in those days was an idolater. However, since the name of the Holy One, blessed be He, is 'Shalom' (Shabbat 10b), one should not double it and say 'shalom, shalom' to him, for doubling 'shalom' is meant only for kings, or for Jews, who are called the children of kings (Gittin 62b). Therefore, if he knows that the gentile will greet him in Hebrew with 'shalom', it is better that he greet him first with 'shalom', so as not to create a situation in which the gentile greets him first with 'shalom' and then, perhaps out of courtesy, he will need to reply 'shalom, shalom' (SA 148:9-10; Levush; Taz).

Just as it is forbidden to give a gift to an idolater on his festival day, so too it is forbidden to receive a gift from him on his festival day, for the idolater will come to thank his idol also for the Jew's having accepted his gift. And if the Jew has no way of evading it, he may accept the gift politely in order to prevent enmity (Avoda Zara 6b; Rambam 9:2).8

The great Rishonim ruled that the Christians of their time were not devout in idolatry, and therefore, when courtesy calls for it, it is permitted to give them a gift or to receive a gift from them on their festival day, and it is likewise permitted to greet them with 'shalom'. But one should not go to their homes to greet them on their festival day, for a Jew should not take part in a festival of gentiles, and courtesy does not obligate him to go to the home of his gentile acquaintance on his festival day to greet him (SA 148:12; Shakh 12).

The same law applies to most Hindus today: although their worship is saturated with idols, since in principle they accept belief in a supreme God, they are not devout in idolatry (above 8:4). Therefore, when courtesy calls for it, it is permitted to give them a gift and to greet them on their festival day, and it is likewise permitted to receive a gift from them on their festival day (Responsa Zivḥei Tzedek He-ḥadashot 3:133).9

sections.title: Three Types of Gentile Festivals
sections.html:
There are three types of gentile festivals: 1) Religious festivals, which a Jew is forbidden to celebrate, whether with gentiles or with Jews. Even if they are celebrated without any religious symbol, it is a Torah prohibition to participate in such a celebration, as it is stated (Vayikra 18:3): "And you shall not walk in their statutes." Examples of religious festivals: Christmas and Easter of the Christians, and the Feast of the Sacrifice of the Muslims and the Druze.

2) Civil holidays that were originally religious festivals, such as 1 January as the marking of the new foreign year: as long as they are celebrated without any religious reference, there is no prohibition in them, but it is not fitting for Jews to celebrate gentile holidays. And when there is a need, such as within the framework of a business party marking the end of the business year, or in order to prevent young Jews from celebrating with gentiles, it is permitted to hold a celebration on it. However, when the party is called 'Sylvester', it becomes a religious festival, which is forbidden to hold because of the statutes of the gentiles (ḥukot ha-goyim).

3) Clearly civil holidays may be celebrated, such as Thanksgiving in North America and 'Novy God' for immigrants from the former Soviet Union. However, it is forbidden to include in them symbols that recall the statutes of the gentiles, such as setting up a fir tree for 'Novy God'. But if they set up a potted plant of a different kind, there will be no prohibition in this. It is fitting for immigrants from the Soviet Union who celebrate 'Novy God' to give it a meaning grounded in values, and to mark it as a day of thanksgiving for having merited to immigrate to the Land and to add their important contribution to the building of the nation.10

Even civil holidays that may be celebrated may not be celebrated in a gentile framework. For the Sages forbade drinking an alcoholic beverage or participating in a feast of gentiles, in order to preserve the separation required between Israel and the nations so as to prevent assimilation. The prohibition has two parts: drinking alcohol, and a party. 1) It is forbidden to drink alcohol with a gentile even in a secular framework, such as at a business meal or simply in the middle of the day. Even when several Jews are present and they brought the drink from home, if most of those gathered are gentiles, it is forbidden to drink alcohol there. However, Jews are permitted to taste kosher refreshments. 2) Within the framework of a party that includes a meal, such as a wedding, it is forbidden to taste even kosher foods (Peninei Halakha, Kashrut 29:12).

sections.title: The Fir Tree, Symbols of Gentile Festivals, and Shopping
sections.html:
The fir tree that Christians customarily set up around the beginning of the foreign year is a custom of a Christian festival, and therefore Jews are forbidden to place a fir tree in their home, office or shop, because of the prohibition of "And you shall not walk in their statutes." The law of all other distinct festival symbols that members of the various religions customarily set up, such as a 'Santa Claus' doll, is like the law of the fir tree.

However, since the fir tree and the other festival symbols are not used for worship, they are not considered idolatry, and therefore when there is a need a Jew may supply them to gentiles. For example, a Jew who has a shop in which he is asked to sell fir trees toward the beginning of the foreign year may sell them in his shop. Likewise, a Jew who is responsible for the maintenance of a building belonging to gentiles and is asked to set up a fir tree for them may set it up (see Shevet Ha-levi 10:132; Mareh Ha-bazak 3:110). A Jew who owns a printing house may carry out an order to print greeting cards for their festivals, since the card involves no expression of worship (Masoret Moshe 4:52).

It is permitted to shop at fairs and sales held in the lead-up to gentile festivals. This applies even to products that are sold for the needs of their festivals, if they are not designated specifically for the needs of their festivals, such as coloured candles, electric bulbs in various colours, and flower decorations made of paper and plastic (above 11:6). It is even permitted to use them for the needs of a mitzva, such as decorating the sukka. Likewise, candles sold at these fairs and sales may be used for the mitzva of Ḥanukka candles (above 10:11).

sections.title: Yoga, Meditation and Martial Arts
sections.html:
It is permitted to practise yoga exercises, meditation and martial arts, but it is forbidden to add to the exercises ceremonies that imitate the customs of the gentiles. Yoga exercises are various physical postures intended to improve health through balance and control of body and soul. Meditation exercises are techniques intended to focus thought and feeling in order to attain control over them, balance and inner enlightenment. Martial arts are intended to refine the ability to defend and attack, and in the process to improve health and attain self-control and a high level of concentration.

Although in the past these exercises were connected to idolatrous religions, since they are performed outside a framework of worship, there is no prohibition in them. But it is forbidden to add to the exercises ceremonies that have no clear and tangible benefit and that consequently express a foreign culture; therefore they are forbidden by Torah law, as it is stated (Vayikra 18:3): "And you shall not walk in their statutes." A 'statute of the gentiles' (ḥok goyim) is a custom expressing cultural-religious symbols that has become entrenched among one of the nations, to the point that it has become a binding practice for them. The Torah forbade Israel to do it, so that Israel will preserve their uniqueness and spiritual independence and not be drawn after the culture and faith of the gentiles and abandon the mitzvot of the Torah (below 28:1).

Therefore, it is permitted to bow to the teacher at the beginning of practice, in the way it is customary to show respect to a teacher in his presence. But it is forbidden to bow before a picture of the teacher before practice, since bowing to a picture is a custom of the gentiles. Likewise, it is forbidden to perform exercises specifically facing the sun, but it is permitted to perform the same exercises when the teacher and the students are not particular about the direction they face. Likewise, it is forbidden to participate in a special initiation ceremony in which the meditation practitioner receives a mantra from the teacher. Similarly, it is forbidden while practising meditation to recite mantras consisting of unintelligible words and sentences in a foreign language.

If the teacher mentions the names of idols, there is an additional prohibition of causing the names of idols to be mentioned in a respectful manner, as it is stated (Shemot 23:13): "And the name of other gods you shall not mention; it shall not be heard from your mouth." But it is permitted to say the names of the exercises in a foreign language, and there is no need to be concerned that they are names of idols, since in practice they serve as names of exercises.

It is important to emphasize that even one who does not transgress any prohibition must take care that these exercises not become the spiritual centre of his life, but rather serve as tools that assist faith in God, the refinement of character traits and the fulfilment of the mitzvot of the Torah. For there is a profound difference between the outlooks: according to the outlook underlying yoga and meditation, the goal is to attain tranquillity and inner enlightenment while disengaging from the challenge of repairing the world, whereas according to the Jewish outlook the vision is the repair of the world (tikkun olam), and health, emotional balance and tranquillity are tools that can help realize the vision (see above, chapter 8).11

sections.title: Various Customs
sections.html:
The greeting 'namaste' is a common greeting in Hindu culture when meeting a person or parting from him. It is generally said with a slight bow while pressing the palms of the hands together. The literal translation of 'namaste' is "I bow to your feet," and its meaning in Vedic literature is "I bow to the holiness within you." Halakhically, just as one may greet a person with the customary greetings in all other languages, so one may greet a person with 'namaste'. The content of this greeting has no idolatrous meaning, because there is truth in it, for in every person there is a divine spark that is worthy of honour. However, it is preferable for Jews to greet with 'shalom', which is the name of the Holy One, blessed be He (Shabbat 10b), and with which Jews customarily greet. The meaning of the greeting 'shalom' is that through the encounter between two people who have a soul within them, mutual enrichment and completion are created, and thereby the name of God is revealed in the world (below 22:10, regarding the greeting of shalom).

There is no prohibition in wearing a Shamballa bracelet, hanging a 'mandala', which is a picture with geometric shapes, or decorating with a potted plant called 'lucky bamboo'. Although idolaters believed that using them grants calm and healing through mystical powers, when one relates to them as attractive decorations that induce calm thanks to the evident effect of their shape and colours, there is no prohibition in them.

Symbols of the Hindu religion printed on bags and various products have the same law as a cross printed as an emblem on stamps and national flags without a religious context, in which there is no prohibition. However, the more recognizable and known they are as expressing a foreign religion, the more preferable it is not to use them, or to remove them; but one who wishes to leave them is not committing a prohibition (as explained above 12:11).

'Voodoo' dolls are used in certain countries in Africa for sorcery or for channelling certain energies, mainly in order to harm others, and sometimes also in order to heal. One who uses them for these purposes transgresses the Torah prohibition of sorcery. One who does not believe in the ability to perform sorcery with them does not transgress a prohibition by keeping them, but it is right not to keep them as decoration, for it is not fitting to decorate the house with something that some people use in a forbidden way.
